In that model the centre of the mixing zone at a drain always stays within 0.1 m of the drain depth, so seepage moves the lens between the drains, and recharge and drainage depth control it alongside seepage (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3659, 3671, 3673–3674); in the model a poorly permeable layer below the drains thins the lens between them and one above them thickens it (p. 3674), and unripened clay, a poorly permeable layer, lies close to the surface over a large part of the island (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 32, 55). A delay, its length open: in that model, started fully saline, 30 years of simulation sufficed for every run to become stationary (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3665), an upper bound; no source read gives how fast the lens follows a change in seepage.

A seedbed in soil with its structure lets the crops germinate better, with less resowing, and yields rise, most for crops sensitive to structure: on flooded clay in Zeeland, plots whose structure gypsum restored yielded up to 15% more sugar beet, 8% more onions and, on heavy clay, up to twice the summer barley, while cereals on light soil gained little (van Beekom et al., 1953b, p. 234, Table 9). Part of the gain is the longer time to work the soil, the link through Spring workability of the fields. Within the year.

Fresh water supplied from outside adds to what crops can draw on: the island's farming depends on the rain that falls and is stored in the root zone or underground, and none is brought in (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 4), which leaves farms short of water in dry periods (p. 8). How much of a supply reaches crops depends on how it is spread: in a design estimate by an engineering consultancy for Provincie Zeeland, a supply through the island's ditches needs 5 m3/s, of which about 2.8 m3/s is pumped back out at the drainage pumping stations (Witteveen+Bos, 2021, p. 40), and it picks up salt from saline seepage on the way (p. 45), to an estimated average of 500 to 800 mg Cl/l at sprinkling against 95 to 500 mg Cl/l at the three sources considered (p. 42), figures the study calls only a very rough indication (pp. 40, 43), above the 300 mg Cl/l damage threshold of salt-sensitive crops (p. 45). A ring pipeline needs 2 m3/s and sprinkles at the source's quality (pp. 42, 45). Within the season.

Active infiltration adds winter water to the lens, on the creek ridges, the dunes and where a sand layer lies under the clay: the creek-ridge infiltration system raises the groundwater through the drains in winter so the lens grows, and the Freshmaker and underground storage inject winter water through a deep drain or a well, all to pump in summer (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 20–22, 38, for the island). What limits it on most of the island is fresh water to infiltrate, since the surface water is mostly saline and drain water the likeliest source (pp. 38, 43, 55), and the rules, under which infiltrating needs a permit as a rule (pp. 26, 45, 54–55; Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026f, art. 4.5 lid 2). Years to a decade, so a delay: on the island's own creek ridge, infiltration with controlled drainage added about 60,000 m³ of fresh water under a 9.5-ha field in ten years and thickened the lens by up to 3.5 m (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 44, a groundwater model of 2020–2050); under a creek ridge on Walcheren, raising the winter water table 0.5 m thickened a 13–15 m lens by 6–8 m in ten years, and the lens had not reached its new thickness yet (Pauw et al., 2015, pp. 1424–1425, 1429, a model result, which transfers since the island's sandy creek ridges also take in rain over saline groundwater: de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3673).

Measures in the low polders keep rain in the field instead of draining it off: controlled drainage and anti-salinisation drainage raise the drains' outflow level, so more water stays in the ground of the field (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 17–18, 29, for the island). On the island's trials raising the drains' outflow level did not plainly keep the water in the field: at Kerkwerve raising the control well barely raised the existing drains' level on one strip, so their discharge fell only very slightly (Oude Essink et al., 2018, p. 91), and near Dreischor, where on one of the two anti-salinisation plots the groundwater never rose to the raised outflow level and the drains did not flow, the authors suspect the groundwater flows away elsewhere (van Hateren et al., 2025, p. 58). Double drainage catches rain rather than keeping it in the field: on two pilots near Kerkwerve its shallow drains carried off 43 to 52% of the winter's net rain to be caught, with little influence on groundwater levels (van Hateren et al., 2025, pp. 4, 77). Within the year.

What farmers pump beyond what the rain puts back thins the lens, the boundary with the saline groundwater below rising: the water board's limit of 800 m³ per hectare a year rests on the balance between recharge by rain, irrigation water and extraction, set to keep the fresh groundwater in stock and the fresh-salt boundary from rising (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b), and pumping too fast risks salinisation (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 20–21). Within those rules the effects are meant to stay within the farm's field, with in principle no depletion, and Deltares's modelling of the rules (2018) found that in general they seem enough to prevent strong salinisation under and around the well (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021, for Zeeland). How fast the lens responds to pumping, no source read shows. In one pilot at Sirjansland, a deep drain pumped about 4,500 m³ a year for two years from a lens thinner than the 15 m the rules require: after the first season the deep monitoring wells showed no salinisation at the bottom or edge of the lens, and after the second geophysical measurements showed the EC at 11 m depth rising, possibly a sign that the pumping shifted the fresh-salt boundary, in data strongly affected by the wet years 2023 and 2024 (Acacia Water, n.d., a consultancy testing with the grower whether small lenses can be managed sustainably, funded by the European Commission and the Province of Zeeland). Its model finds the resistance of any separating layers important for the calculated upconing of saline water, with more to pump where it is higher (Acacia Water, n.d.), and under the creek ridges in the east of the island the deeper subsoil to about 25 m is mostly fine sand with local thin clay layers (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 38).

The more a well pumps from the lens, the further salt groundwater rises towards it: in the Freshmaker pilot at Ovezande, Zuid-Beveland, the water pumped from the shallow well grew saltier as each pumping season went on (Oude Essink et al., 2018, p. 67). The report on the island's freshwater measures lists salinisation at too high a pumping rate as a risk of the creek-ridge infiltration system and of underground storage (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 20–21). Within the year: the cone follows the season's pumping.

A larger harvest per hectare raises income at a given price, the price being World prices of conventional crops. The + holds in full where only the island's yield falls, to salt or a local shortage of fresh water. A dry summer across north-west Europe also raises the price, since the harvests there set it: for potatoes, north-west Europe is one market, and their price was highest in the extremely dry 2018 (Janssens et al., 2020, p. 8). Then what a farm loses depends on how it sells: in 2018, higher prices could help onion growers make up for a harvest forecast 44% below the year before, while potato growers mostly held contracts at prices agreed in advance (NOS, 2018), some 80% of the crop at around nine cents a kilo while free-market potatoes reached 30 (DutchNews.nl, 2018); onions are rarely sold under such contracts (Bogosavac, 2018). On the island, a farm with its own stored water can gain from the high prices of a dry year (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 36). For seed potatoes, 8% of the island's cropping plan in 2021 (Delphy, 2023, p. 42), the price is set mainly by size grade, with the coarse sizes paid much less, so a lack of water at tuber set gives fewer tubers, often made up in kilograms by larger ones that are poorly paid (Delphy, 2023, p. 44, advisers' judgement in a report commissioned by the island's farmers' association). For them the + holds for the kilograms in the best-paid sizes, 28–50 mm, not for weight alone (p. 44). Within the year, as the harvest is sold.

A fall in the land's value that has happened, through salt in R8: does a farm whose land lost value object harder to the next plan? Through its solvency, yes (−); where compensation pays more than the land would fetch on the market, the concern may fall instead (+). A hypothesis for the group model building session, with both signs as the question to farmers.
connections.simplification: Folds Owners' concern about their land's value, which gathered the reasons for objecting: a fall in the land's value, and a plan that would lower it, raised landowning farmers' concern, and the concern raised their objections. The sign is the product of the two steps, so R8 keeps its polarity, and the concern was no actor's decision of its own. A tenant's concern, losing the lease, was never part of it. What it leaves out: why owners object is no variable on the drawing, a question for the group model building session.

connections.description: With the same debt, a lower land value is a higher debt relative to the farm's assets: land is 70% of an arable farm's balance sheet (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 13), and its rise in value is what made arable farms' solvency 81% in 2018 (p. 21). A high solvency can let a farm borrow more and at a lower rate (p. 19); the debt itself does not shrink when the land loses value. It holds for the land a farm owns: farms owning little of it barely gain from a rising price (p. 26). While land rose the ratio moved little: from 2006 to 2015 Dutch arable farms' balance sheet per farm doubled, mainly through the rise in the land price, while their solvency rose only from 76% to 78% and their bank loans went from just over 5,000 to 10,000 euro per ha, an unchanged 16% share (Silvis et al., 2017, p. 2, national farm accounts). The note was commissioned by a.s.r. vastgoed vermogensbeheer (p. 4). Within the year: the farm accounts value the land each year (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 13).

For every loan a bank must hold capital, as the law on banks' solvency sets, the more the higher the credit risk, and the cost of that capital, the return its shareholders require, is part of the interest each client pays (ABN AMRO, n.d.-a). The final Basel III standards raise that capital, EU banks' minimum Tier 1 capital requirement by an estimated 9.0% at full implementation in 2028 (European Banking Authority, 2023). Together the two make stricter capital rules raise what a bank charges for a loan. Measured across EU banks: no source read gives the change for Dutch farm loans. Within the year: the bank prices the capital with each loan.

Soil work for potatoes should not be done when the soil is too wet, which can smear and compact it; for onions, too-wet soil work can keep a well-crumbled seedbed from forming, and in March and April, as the scenarios' rain rises, unfavourable conditions for it may become more likely; where blight cannot be well controlled, as in organic farming, a potato crop is best planted early where the soil allows (Verstand et al., 2021, pp. 25, 27, for the Netherlands, from a cultivation guide, a crop study and an expert). So, by inference from that guide, the more of the rotation they take, the more farmers need fields that dry early in spring. Holding water back longer, as a buffer for dry times, is sometimes hard for farmers who want onto the land with heavy machinery (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021c, p. 44); on Duiveland the board moves to the higher summer level in March and April as the soil work allows (2021a, p. 66). No source read shows how much spring soil work the new crops need: the sign rests on their needing less. Quinoa, a salt-tolerant crop, also needs soil work in spring: in the Netherlands it is sown from the end of March to the end of April and needs a fine seed bed (van Loo, 2023, pp. 75, 77, by a Wageningen breeder whose group develops quinoa varieties), so the sign holds where the share moves to crops sown in autumn or winter, such as winter wheat, sown from mid-September to early February (Verstand et al., 2021, p. 29), less clearly where it moves to quinoa; and on clay and zavel, the main topsoil of the island's western low polders (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 27), the main soil work for potatoes is often done before winter (Verstand et al., 2021, p. 25). Within the year.
A farm that relies on high margins can give fewer hectares to lower-margin new crops.

More income from the land raises what buyers bid for it, through what they expect an extra hectare to earn an expanding farm over the years of the investment rather than through last year's income (Farjon et al., 2013, box Maximale biedprijs; Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, pp. 2–3). The + holds beside drivers the island's farms cannot move: since 1970 the nominal Dutch price has risen more than tenfold while net value added rose two- to threefold, carried by scale enlargement and falling interest rates (Farjon et al., 2013, introduction and section Ontwikkeling van de prijs). Across individual land transactions in the Netherlands from 2004 to 2011, the expected revenue from the land had a significant positive effect on the price, beside land regulations, the spatial environment and local market conditions (Boere, 2015, pp. 81, 98). Years: its swings ran over years, the real price rising sharply and then falling by half in the late 1970s and by 30% between 1995 and 2005 (Farjon et al., 2013, section Ontwikkeling van de prijs): a delay.

More income leaves more, after the household's spending and the farm's payment obligations, repayments included, to save for investment; a negative income leaves too little to reserve, and machines then age (Verhagen et al., 2018, pp. 23, 25). A farm with good solvency can probably take up extra credit when its income is negative, the same report judges, and Dutch arable farms averaged close to 80% solvency in 2015, land more than two thirds of their balance sheet (Verhagen et al., 2018, pp. 23, 25; national farm accounts, no figure for the island), so a poor year may shrink what a solvent farm can invest less than its income. A lasting low income is harder to bridge: the bank looks hard at long-term continuity before deferring payments or giving extra credit (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 28), and in a simulation of banks' credit checks, which base a new loan on the past three years' net cash flow, solvency was the limit in only 1.2% of farm observations and net cash flow in almost all cases (Lamkowsky, 2023, pp. 51–52, 56, 101; Dutch dairy farms, 2009–2017). Within the year: income adds to the savings in the year it is earned.
Capacity to invest decides whether a farm can pay for a storage measure, not whether it wants to.

Capacity to invest decides whether a farm can pay for the switch (new machines, the first years of a new crop), not whether it wants to. The costs of salt-tolerant seed and soil amendments may not make up for the yield and income salt takes in the first years, when setting up costs most, and the benefits are not always obvious in the short term (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 60); farms whose financial buffers shrank in the corona crisis were expected to be less willing to invest, slowing their modernisation and sustainability, and banks often count financing a new concept whose returns are not yet proven as a risk (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 6). For samphire and sea aster the outlet, not only capacity to invest, limits adoption: their food market is small and easily saturated, in the authors' judgement (van den Burg et al., 2024, p. 6), and growers in Zeeland's saline cultivation, eight in all, say there is little room for new entrants, and that making room would also take strong growth of the market for saline vegetables (Delphy, 2023, p. 49, a consultancy report commissioned by Agrarisch Schouwen Duiveland that argues for a freshwater supply, p. 50). Delphy adds that cheaper imports compete and that few of Zeeland's soils suit these crops, but sees openings in high-end restaurants and retail if the season can be lengthened, and in other saline crops less grown abroad (p. 49). Within the year: the crop is chosen each season.

Higher temperatures and drier weather raise evapotranspiration, the water crops use when they have enough, highest in sunny, warm and dry weather (Allen et al., 1998, FAO-56). Once a crop has drawn the root zone down beyond the water it can take up easily, it uses less water than it needs, in proportion to what is left in the root zone (Allen et al., 1998, ch. 8): the shortfall is the part of the demand that rain, soil moisture and irrigation leave unmet, so the more the crops need, the larger it is. On Schouwen-Duiveland's clay a crop that has come up well gets through the summer on the soil's good supply of moisture, so the shortfall falls mostly at germination early in the season, when a small gift of about 20 mm would cover it; onions also need water while they grow (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 27, 31, 38, from talks with the island's farmers). Within the year.
connections.simplification: Folds Crop water demand, a step between the two with no actor and no decision: hotter, drier summers raise what crops need, and what they need beyond the water they get is the shortfall. The sign is the product of the two steps (+, then +). Hotter, drier summers is a Constant, so no loop runs through the link. What it leaves out: what crops need is no variable of its own, so a crop's own water need, new crops against the current ones, cannot enter; no source read shows whether the new crops need less.

connections.description: Rain, irrigation and capillary rise from the groundwater add water to the root zone and lower its depletion; once the depletion passes the readily available water, the crop uses less water than it needs (Allen et al., 1998, FAO-56 ch. 8, eqs. 84–85, a daily water balance). So the more fresh water crops can draw on, the smaller the shortfall, within the season. On the island's farms a gift of 20 to 25 mm at germination can make the difference where none can be given now (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 27, 55). In the low western polders (Scharendijke–Brouwershaven–Kerkwerve) the farmers in the project's quickscans find drought a problem mainly at germination: once the crop has come up well, the soil's good moisture supply keeps drought damage later in summer limited even in dry years, and waterlogging is often felt as the larger problem (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 27), though a study paid for by the island's farmers' association assumes a much larger water need (Delphy, 2023, p. 40). How much extra water eases also depends on crop and year: raising the water table by subirrigation on a test field at Rusthoeve on Noord-Beveland, on sandy clay (zavel) with saline seepage, raised dry-matter yield against a reference field by 18 % for onions in dry 2022 but by 2 to 7 % for chicory in dry 2020 and for wheat and potato in normal-to-wet 2021 (Terink et al., 2023, p. 44, a trial by KnowH2O and KWR paid for by the province, the water board and the municipality of Noord-Beveland).

Farmers pump more fresh groundwater as the shortfall grows: the water board registered a considerable increase in extractions in recent years, which the more extreme drought certainly influenced, so the volume pumped rises in dry years (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021, for Zeeland, whose farms pump under the same rules as the island's). On Schouwen-Duiveland the farms get their fresh water from rain and from the fresh groundwater; the shallow groundwater and the surface water hold high salt levels, and no fresh water can be brought in during dry periods (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 8). Without a permit they may pump where the water board's map shows a fresh groundwater body outside its vulnerable areas, one at least 15 m thick or reaching the geohydrological base (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026f, arts. 1.1 and 4.8 b), which lies under the creek ridges and the dunes (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10): in the low polders the farmers talked to do not sprinkle, some trying drip irrigation, while on a creek ridge a livestock farmer pumps from two deep drains for grassland in the summer season, more in dry years, and an arable farmer occasionally irrigates about 20 mm at germination, the report not saying where that water comes from (pp. 27–28, 40, 43). So the link runs where a farm has fresh groundwater under it. The rules cap each well's pumping: under Waterschap Scheldestromen's general rule a well may take at most 800 m³ a year per hectare of its parcel (80 mm) and 8,000 m³ a year, a permit with conditions being possible where a well cannot meet them (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b, art. 2.9 and its explanation). For the creek ridges of the south-western delta, Deltares researchers presenting a system to enlarge their fresh lenses stated in 2015, under the rules of that time, that irrigation demand already exceeded the permissible extraction, which led to crop damage (Pauw et al., 2015, p. 1415, a statement, not a measurement), so in a dry summer a growing shortfall may end in crop damage rather than in more pumping. Within the year.

What farmers pump is fresh water their crops get: what pumping gains them. In the study's options for the island it goes onto the field by reel sprinkler or by drip, and the method influences how much of it the crop gets: drip loses less water, so a cubic metre covers more land, while a reel usually gives several gifts per hectare (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 35, in its cost-benefit analysis for the island's farms). On a cluster of three farms on a creek ridge, a livestock farmer irrigates grassland in dry years, in midsummer too, from two deep drains under a permit of up to 16,000 m³ a year (pp. 40, 43). Across the whole island it is a small flow: a water balance from model output and the water board's permits puts groundwater irrigation at 0.33 million m³ a summer half-year, taken at the permitted maximum since what is actually pumped is unknown, against a precipitation deficit of about 30 million m³ in the dry summer of 2018 (Krajenbrink et al., 2023, pp. 44, 46, 48; the authors call the irrigation figures probably inaccurate and the groundwater irrigation of 2018 still on the low side, pp. 45, 47). Of what a reel sprays, about 60% went to crop growth on potatoes and onions, against 80 to 90% for drip on onions, measured at Philippine in Zeeuws-Vlaanderen with the farmer sprinkling in the evening and not in wind, in a project with an irrigation firm in its team (Acacia Water, 2020, pp. ii, 7, 25). The salt a well may draw up with the water runs through Upconing of salt groundwater. Within the season: within the year, no delay.

A crop that uses less water than it needs yields less, in proportion: its relative yield falls by a crop's yield response factor times its relative shortfall in evapotranspiration, over the season 1.1 for potatoes and onions, 1.0 for sugar beet and 1.05 for winter wheat, the loss small in the vegetative and ripening periods and large in flowering and yield formation (Allen et al., 1998, FAO-56 ch. 8, eq. 90 and Table 24, after FAO paper 33, general). On the island, farmers in the western low polders find the shortfall falls mostly at germination, and a crop that emerged well loses little to drought later in the summer (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 27); a potato grower at Nieuwerkerk lost a fifth of his 2026 harvest, the potatoes smaller too, when growth stopped in the June heat and the rain came too late, the water in many of Zeeland's ditches too saline to irrigate from and the region short of fresh water (van Essen, 2026). In a water-need study for the island paid for by the farmers' association Agrarisch Schouwen Duiveland, Delphy's south-west arable advisers count only a quarter of the season's shortfall towards the water need of sugar beet and winter wheat, whose long growing season lets them make up a shortfall later with strong growth, and half for grass seed and ware potatoes, mostly late ones, which compensate somewhat less, late ware potatoes still giving reasonable yields in dry years through rain late in the season (Delphy, 2023, pp. 1, 32). These factors come from Delphy's experience in practice, and Delphy calls the result still fairly optimistic, since drought may also fall at other moments, later in the summer or at tuber set (Delphy, 2023, p. 33). Within the season.

Income is what is left of revenue after the costs paid and depreciation, plus extraordinary items (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 21, from national farm accounts), and irrigating is one of a farm's costs: in the cost study for the island's farms, one irrigation gift of 20–25 mm by reel costs about €200, and surface drip irrigation €1,000 a hectare (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 35), figures the study takes from earlier work, not measured in it. Within the year.

A supply route carries fresh water to the island: since the island is not connected to the main freshwater system, no fresh water can be brought to it in dry periods (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 8). What a route delivers depends on its source: two of the three sources explored lie in the Volkerak-Zoommeer, the third is the Haringvliet (Witteveen+Bos, 2021, p. 7, for Provincie Zeeland), and algae stop the inlets from that lake, on Tholen in seven of the years 2003–2011 and on average from 20 July, and, as algae growth declines, at the factsheet's writing (2013) only from about mid-August (Schipper et al., 2014, p. 36, a factsheet for Tholen), and in July 2026 rising blue-green algae there led Waterschap Brabantse Delta to ban taking surface water in two polders, the Prins Hendrikpolder and the Auvergnepolder, fed from the lake, through the Schelde-Rijnkanaal among others, which have no other supply route (Waterschap Brabantse Delta, 2026, p. 1). Within the year, once a route exists.

Dry summers lower the discharge of the great rivers, and drought more often brings a water shortage, in which the scarce water is divided among drinking water, nature, agriculture and shipping (KNMI, 2023, p. 42, the Planbureau voor de Leefomgeving's risks for the Netherlands, measured nationally): a route can only carry what summer discharge and the national distribution in drought (the verdringingsreeks, IenW and Rijkswaterstaat) leave for the region, outside the CLD's scale. Within the year: a summer's discharge sets that summer's supply.
connections.simplification: Folds Fresh water available for supply in drought: dry summers leave less river water for a supply route, and the route carries what is left. The sign is the product of the two steps (−, then +). Hotter, drier summers is a Constant, so no loop runs through the link. What it leaves out: the river water left for the region in drought, which the national distribution decides outside the CLD's scale, is no variable of its own.

connections.description: Damage from drought is why, the report says, the farming sector presses for a pipeline to the island (Witteveen+Bos, 2021, p. 7), and ZLTO's branch there called for one after a report on the shortage (Omroep Zeeland, 2023). No delay drawn: how quickly a dry summer turns into a call, no source read shows.

The body deciding on a route weighs the call; so far a study has followed and no route has been decided on (Freshwater supply route to the island). Years, so a delay: a route has to be decided on and paid for, and implementing its pipeline alone is expected to take about 3 to 10 years (Freshwater supply route to the island).

Clay that has lost its structure stays wet long into spring, so it can be worked only late and the time to make a seedbed is very short; restored with gypsum, it dries sooner and can be worked for a longer period (van Beekom et al., 1953b, pp. 233–234, on clay in Zeeland flooded by the sea in 1944–45, the sodium breaking down the structure as in Clay dispersion & sodification). Within the year.

The deeper the ditch levels lie below the fields, the sooner the fields drain and dry after rain. By the water board's rules for its whole area, the drooglegging is set at an optimum for each use and soil, against both wet and drought damage (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 7); at half the design discharge it must keep a field's drains, laid at their optimal depth, all but above the ditch water (p. 8); and an area 10 cm or more short of its optimum counts as too wet (p. 9). Once the drooglegging reaches that optimum the drains already lie clear of the ditch water by the rule above, so a deeper level should, by inference, add little workability; on Duiveland the board's model test finds the drooglegging more than 40 cm past its optimum (60 cm on schorgronden) in large parts of the area in all situations, against 10 of 31 level areas with more than 10% of their surface too wet in a normal winter and 11 in summer (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, pp. 32, 42). On the Rusthoeve trial farm, measured on Noord-Beveland on zavel with saline seepage and an average drooglegging of 1.6 m, a drain outlet held 30 cm higher raised the groundwater on average 10 cm near the ditch and 20 cm mid-field with no adverse effect on workability, by the farm's experience, on blocks redrained at 6 m instead of about 12 m (Schipper et al., 2015, pp. 6, 15, 17–18, 76; funded by the Province of Zeeland, ZLTO and the water board, along with national and Interreg funds, p. 11). On Duiveland four level areas may run a lower target for a while in wet periods, where the fields' drainage and workability need it (2021a, p. 40), and the move from the winter to the summer level in spring follows the farmers' soil work (p. 66). Within the season, no delay.

Fields that cannot be worked in time are planted late: a later planting date can shorten the potato's growing season, since later in the season it is often too wet to harvest, and where blight cannot be controlled, as in organic farming, it costs yield, so an early date is preferred where the soil allows (Verstand et al., 2021, p. 25, from a crop study and an expert, for the Netherlands). No source read shows it for onions or sugar beet. Within the year.

Where fields stay too wet to work, farmers want lower ditch levels: what deep drainage gains them. In the water board's words, holding water back longer as a buffer for dry times is sometimes hard for farmers who want onto the land with heavy machinery (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021c, p. 44, its management programme for its whole area): the board's account of the farmers' interest, not the farmers' own. No source read shows how much a wet spring raises the demand. The water board's own model test of the current levels, which compares computed ditch levels with the optimum drainage depth for each soil and use and does not measure workability, finds more than 10% of the surface too wet in a normal winter in 9 of the 43 level areas outside nature in Schouwen's polder, but 18 under the summer level, 62% of the area, which the board brings in step by step in March–April (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, pp. 19, 32–36, 44, 56); on Duiveland 10 of 31 tested areas are more than 10% too wet in a normal winter and 11 in summer (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 42). The link so seems to act mainly around that switch and in the wetter areas. Within the year.

A higher ditch level raises the counter-pressure on the salt groundwater, so the seepage pressure falls; a lower level lowers it, so the seepage pressure rises (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 37, the board's analysis for Duiveland's water level plan). The seepage is driven by the higher water pressure at greater depth, in the first aquifer below the polders' clay (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 10–11, 28), and drainage depth is the difference between the surface and the ditch level (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 40), so at the same drainage depth a lower polder has a lower ditch level and the lowest polders get the most: on the island the eastern polders lie somewhat higher than the western ones and so generally have no or far less seepage pressure (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 28), and comparing the island's elevation with a regional groundwater model, seepage occurs in the polders below sea level and rain soaks in on the dunes, the creek ridges and the polders above it, the two strongly correlated (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3661, 3673). A raise in one level area can also lift the head in the shared first aquifer around it, so seepage can rise on the land next to it: in a model of a 110 km2 low-lying polder inundated in 2100, seepage in the polder fell but rose in the adjacent areas, a net cut of only 9% of the polder's salt load (Oude Essink et al., 2010, pp. 8–9, 13–14, modelled in the western Netherlands). On Schouwen's south coast a seepage ditch rings the raised nature area so that its higher level does not add seepage on the land around it (van Haperen et al., 2006, p. 3, Staatsbosbeheer, which manages part of the area, an account without data). Within the year: the water pressures in the top layer change constantly with recharge and drainage (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3675).

The board holds the ditch levels lower in winter than in summer to prevent water damage in winter, and a higher winter level would keep the groundwater from sinking as deep (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 37, its analysis for Duiveland): the deeper the ditches stand in winter, the more of the rain they and the drains carry off. Within the year.

On a creek ridge studied for water storage, where in winter the ditch levels lie over 1.5 m below the surface in large parts, the drains and ditches carry the excess rain off fast, and a higher winter level might raise the groundwater and with it the recharge (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 42–43): so the deeper the drainage, the less of the winter's rain refills the lens, which the source gives as a possibility, not a measurement. Years, so a delay: the lens is a Stock, which on the island's own creek ridge thickened by up to 3.5 m in ten years under infiltration with controlled drainage (p. 44, a groundwater model of 2020–2050).

A water level plan sets the levels the board pursues and maintains in normal circumstances (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021d, 2022), after its procedure: the executive board adopts a draft, open to views for six weeks; the general board adopts the plan; appeal is open for six weeks (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 17–18), for Duiveland from February to August 2021 (2021a, p. 53; 2021d). Its levels take effect on a date the plan sets, which depends partly on the works they need (2025, p. 18): Duiveland's plan proposed studying a raise in 14 level areas, most possible only once the discharge capacity is enlarged (2021a, p. 69), and the works for that were still being put to the island in March 2026 (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026a). In summer the levels a plan sets may not hold: the board's own study for Duiveland says that in many areas, where the winter level is low and the summer level set well above it, the higher summer level can usually be held for a few weeks and then sinks slowly into the soil, depending on location and soil, and that without water supply, which the island lacks (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 8), the summer level may not be maintainable in a rainfall deficit (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, pp. 37, 66). Years, so a delay.

Polder drainage depth is the surface minus the ditch level, the difference on which the board defines its optimum (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 40), so the higher the board holds the level, the less depth the fields have above it. Within the year.

Polder drainage depth is the surface minus the ditch level, the difference on which the board defines its optimum (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 40), so where the land subsides under a level held, the depth shrinks until a new plan lowers the level, as the board's policy describes for peat (2025, p. 13). Within the year: the depth follows the surface, and the slowness sits in the surface's fall (Polder drainage depth → Polder surface elevation (NAP)).

The water board weighs farmers' need for low levels against raising them: it involves farming among the interest groups as it prepares a plan and weighs their input (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 17), and on Duiveland moves to the higher summer level in March and April as the farmers' soil work allows (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 66). How much the farmers' views weigh against the board's other aims, no source read shows: on Duiveland four views against a raise the plan proposed to study did not change the plan (p. 53). The board's guideline tests a level area against a norm: the norm for farmland derives from the optimal drain depths for farming (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 7); with more than 10% of the area too wet the level must be lowered or the discharge's bottlenecks solved, with less a raise is considered (p. 9). On Duiveland, by the board's research report for its plan of 2021, a level change in most level areas is possible only once the discharge capacity is enlarged (2021a, p. 69). Years, so a delay: the board weighs it as it prepares a plan, which it does when its evaluation every three years, weighing among other things the reports of those concerned, finds a plan no longer current, or once a plan is 17 years old (2025, pp. 16–17).

The water board names the gradually increasing salinisation a concern for the fresh water farming needs, the thin fresh groundwater lenses most threatened, and aims to keep or enlarge the lenses: by not lowering target levels much, since a lower level lowers the counter-pressure on the salt groundwater and raises the seepage pressure, while a raise lowers it (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 37, a criterion of its analysis for Duiveland's water level plan). So the more seepage salts the soil's fresh water, the more reason the board has to raise levels, the lens being what it protects (Saline seepage → Rainwater lens thickness in the low polders). On Duiveland the plan of 2021 proposed studying a raise in 14 level areas to enlarge the fresh water in the soil and give crops more moisture (p. 69); how far seepage weighed there against drought, no source read shows. Elsewhere on the island the board gives drought as its reason: on Schouwen, where nearly the whole polder gets seepage, it raises the level in ten level areas to limit drought damage, with larger fresh water stocks in the soil as the effect, its method naming seepage only as a ground to deviate from the guideline that 10% of a level area may be too wet (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, pp. 26, 36–37, 53), and its framework for every level plan from 2025 names neither seepage nor the lenses among its criteria for a raise (2025, pp. 9, 12). So the board's accounts read give the link little support on the island: in them, the Duiveland criterion above is the only stated reason for a raise that names the lenses. Years, so a delay: the board weighs it as it prepares a plan, which it does when its evaluation every three years finds a plan no longer current, or once a plan is 17 years old (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 16–17).
Rising pumping costs give the water board a reason to raise the levels.

By the water board's rules, the views sent on a draft plan within six weeks are answered in the decision, anyone affected may appeal at the court for six weeks after it, and the board consults the region first so that as few conflicts as possible arise to slow or interrupt the procedure (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 17–18). So objections can delay, change or stop a plan to raise the levels while it is pending; with none pending they change nothing, and they never lower a level. On the island the views on the two plans of 2021 changed neither: Duiveland's 25 views from six people (2021a, p. 53) and Schouwen's 11 from five, which added some studies (2021b, pp. 7–8). As the board summarises the views, four on Duiveland's proposed study of a raise gave as their concern that flooding becomes likelier in extreme rain, not the land's value (2021a, p. 53), and its summary of Schouwen's names none against the raises in its ten level areas (2021b, pp. 7–8, 53). The region's reactions before each draft were taken into the work on it (2021a, pp. 52–53; 2021b, p. 7). Whether anyone appealed either plan, no source read shows. Elsewhere in Zeeland a view did change the same board's plan: on the raise of a winter level in the Braakman, near Terneuzen, ZLTO objected for seven farmers that one party's gain should not harm another, and the plan of 2015 took a phased raise, its first step only once the field that suffers most has been acquired and its second within six years (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2015, p. 2). By the board's own rules, damage from a deliberate change of a field's drainage depth that is significant, disproportionate and beyond normal social risk is likely to be compensated, where possible by technical measures or by buying or exchanging land and, failing agreement, by a claim decided apart from the plan with its own objection and appeal (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 14–15, 18); in the Braakman an independent valuer was to assess the expected damage on the field that may suffer disproportionately (2015, p. 2). So where an owner's loss passes that threshold, an objection over it may be answered without dropping the raise, though no source read shows how often that happens. Within the year, as the plan is decided.

Seepage that reaches the ditches is pumped out with the rain: across most of Duiveland the waterways catch salt or brackish seepage from below (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 20); Schouwen's water comes mainly from rain and partly from seepage, strongest at its edges and in the low inlagen (2021b, pp. 25–26), all of it flowing to the pumping stations (2021b, p. 24), as Duiveland's whole area is drained by pumping (2021a, p. 21); and the low western polders, under seepage, drain their brackish to salt water through pumping stations (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 27). The board's electricity cost moves with the water it pumps: in the dry year 2025 its water systems spent €1.1 million less on electricity than budgeted, for the drought, and extreme rain can raise the electricity cost of its sewage and polder pumping stations by up to 25% (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026e, pp. 18, 55); seepage is part of the water pumped, so more seepage costs more, within the year, though the source does not name seepage. No source read gives seepage's share of the water pumped on the island.

The rain drained from the fields flows to the pumping stations, which pump it over the dike (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, pp. 24–25; 2021a, p. 21), and the board's electricity follows it: in the dry year 2025 its water systems spent €1.1 million less on electricity than budgeted, for the drought (2026e, p. 18), and extreme rain can raise its pumping stations' electricity by up to 25% (p. 55), across the board's area. Within the year.

The board passes its pumping costs on through its levy, part of the costs of its water management, of which unbuilt land other than nature carries 22.78% for 2026 (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026c, art. 2). One rate holds across its whole area, so a cost that rises on the island is spread over all of it: the law lets the board charge pumped areas up to 100% more (Waterschapswet, 2026, art. 122), and its ordinance for 2026 does not.

The levy is a cost to the farm that holds the land: the law charges those who hold unbuilt land by ownership, possession or a limited right, not its tenants (Waterschapswet, 2026, art. 117), at one rate per hectare (art. 121), €115.53 for 2026 (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026d, art. 6), and a farm's income is its revenue minus the costs it pays and depreciation (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 21). Whether a tenant pays it through the rent, no source read shows. Within the year: the levy is charged each year.

Once a crop's root zone salinity, as the conductivity of the saturated soil extract (ECe), passes its threshold, its yield falls in proportion to the excess (Allen et al., 1998, ch. 8, eq. 89): onions lose 16% per dS/m above 1.2 dS/m and potatoes 12% above 1.7, rated sensitive and moderately sensitive, against 5.9% above 7.0 for sugar beet and 7.1% above 6.0 for wheat (Table 23), so on the island's rotations salt takes most from potatoes and onions. The harm is osmotic at once and comes from sodium or chloride building up in the leaves more slowly (Munns & Tester, 2008, pp. 654–656). Table 23 is a guideline from experiments mostly under irrigation, the soil kept close to field capacity (Allen et al., 1998, ch. 8), tolerance varying with climate, soil and practice, and crops often less tolerant as they germinate and as seedlings (Table 23, note 1): crop physiology that, by inference, holds on the island's fields too, its thresholds not measured there. Field trials at Salt Farm Texel, on sand irrigated with saline water, find gentler lines for potatoes and onions: across 13 potato cultivars a threshold of 3.2 dS/m and a slope of 6.1% per dS/m on average over the cultivars and years (van Straten et al., 2021, pp. 1, 5), and for onions thresholds of 2.4–5.9 dS/m and slopes of 7.4–11.7% per dS/m, with wide confidence intervals (de Vos et al., 2016, p. 22); both come from the trial farm's own trials, written by its staff with university co-authors, the 2021 one partly funded by the Salt Farm Foundation, and may not hold on clay (de Vos et al., 2016, pp. 2, 9; van Straten et al., 2021, pp. 1, 11). A review for the Deltaprogramma Zoetwater judges that the rule over- or underestimates the loss, not reproducibly, where root-zone salinity varies within the season, as it mostly does in Dutch open-field farming (van Bakel et al., 2018, pp. 30–31): on the island the sign holds, but these lines do not fix the size of the loss. Within the season.

Harvest lost to salt is income lost: at the farm, salt lowers the yield and raises the cost of inputs such as fresh water and soil amendments (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 12). For potatoes north-west Europe should be seen as one market, the size of its harvest showing in the price (Janssens et al., 2020, p. 8), so salt on the island's fields alone does not move it, and a harvest lost to salt is lost at that price. Within the year, as the harvest is sold.

A field moved from a current crop to a new salt-tolerant one no longer has a conventional harvest for salt to take: the link holds by what Harvest lost to salt counts, the fields still under the current crops. The new crops lose less to salt, not nothing: 10 to 19 of the 50 experts and stakeholders interviewed across the Netherlands' salinisation-prone provinces say that, in general, salts affect the soil's structure and so lower yields even where a crop is or becomes more tolerant, and that the salt level at which cultivation on clay stops being effective is largely uncertain (Beauchampet, 2022, pp. 213–214, 221, interviews, not measurements); the island's polders generally have clayey soils (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10). Within the year, from the next season's crop.
connections.simplification: The new crops are taken to lose nothing to salt. That comes nearest to true for crops that can be grown on saline land, such as sea fennel and sea banana on an arable farm at Colijnsplaat (EU CAP Network, 2023), and for quinoa, among the crops better suited to saline conditions, though how far salt limits a crop depends on the crop (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 63). A new crop as sensitive as the current ones loses about as much, and R6 does not run through it.

connections.description: A salt-tolerant variety loses less of its harvest at the same salinity of the root zone: in field trials on Texel from 2012 to 2018, most potato cultivars kept 90% of their yield up to a soil salinity (ECe) of about 4 to 5 dS/m, some about twice that (van Straten et al., 2021, pp. 1–2), Elgar and Rivola above 7.5 dS/m (p. 10). Measured on sandy soil, the salt brought by irrigation water: the sign holds on the island, since the trials relate yield to the salinity of the root zone, which drives Harvest lost to salt there whatever brings the salt; the size need not, as the authors warn for other soils and climates (p. 11). Past the salinity at which they keep 90% of their yield, Elgar and Rivola lose yield faster than the other cultivars, in estimates whose large uncertainties, the authors note, make significant differences between cultivars hard to find (van Straten et al., 2021, p. 6); a larger ECe90 goes with a steeper decline, so all cultivars reach about the same lethal soil salinity, 20–24 dS/m (pp. 1, 5), and the advantage narrows as salinity approaches it. The study was partly funded by the Salt Farm Foundation (p. 11).

A hectare moved from a high-margin current crop to a new one earns the new crop's margin instead, and the margin of protein crops cannot compete with most other crops (Polman et al., 2026, p. 9). The link holds by what the element counts, the hectares taken from the high-margin crops: the area of protein crops, rarely a farm's main crop, likely depends on the room left in the rotation (Polman et al., 2026, p. 17), and in a simulation for Flanders quinoa mostly took the place of maize and winter wheat (Cloet et al., 2024, p. 3). On the island without extra fresh water, a scenario calculation for a model 100 ha farm with prices held fixed, in a report commissioned and co-financed by the island's farmers' association Agrarisch Schouwen Duiveland, puts the margin of sown onions in the 2022 crop plan at €1,197 a hectare, at 25 tonnes against 60 with enough fresh water, below grain's €1,348 and far below the €6,635 of potatoes for processing, and expects onions to shrink or leave the island by 2030 (Delphy, 2023, pp. 1, 3, 42–45). A field moved from onions then gives up little, drought losses being counted in the current crop's margin. Within the year: the crop is chosen each season.

A tolerant variety earns less than the variety it replaces where salt does not limit the crop: salt-tolerant varieties are usually lower yielding, high-yielding varieties being sensitive to stress through a trade-off between tolerance and yield (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 30). In greenhouse pots at Wageningen in 2024, a salt-tolerant potato variety lost 18% of its tuber weight under salt against 39% for a sensitive one (p. 21), yet on fresh water it netted about €1,800 a hectare with the soil amendment that served it best, against about €2,300 for the sensitive, high-yielding variety grown as usual (pp. 51–52). So the margin given up is largest on fresh land. Measured in pots, which the authors recommend repeating in the open field (p. 52). Within the year: the variety is chosen each season.

Margin given up is income given up, in full: a margin is what a crop leaves after its variable costs (Cloet et al., 2024, p. 1), and the farm's fixed costs do not fall when its storage crops take a smaller part of the rotation, the buildings, machines and paving being sunk (Polman et al., 2026, p. 17). In full may be an upper end over the long run: in Dutch farm accounts for 2014–2022, farms with a larger share of ware and seed potatoes, onions and winter carrots carry significantly higher non-allocated costs per hectare (Polman et al., 2026, p. 15), but changes within a farm over the years explain little of these costs, the explained variation lying between farms, and the estimate, by the authors' account biased and less reliable, is available only from the authors on request (pp. 5, 12–13). Within the year, as the harvest is sold.

Higher prices for the current crops raise the income from them: a farm's income is its revenue minus the costs it pays and depreciation (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 21), and Dutch arable farms' income fell to an estimated 60,000 euro per unpaid labour unit in 2025 on lower prices, after favourable growing conditions and higher yields in north-west Europe and beyond, slightly rising costs adding to the fall (van der Meulen, 2025). How far a farm's income follows the price depends on how it sells (World prices of conventional crops). Measured nationally. Within the year, as the harvest is sold.
As harvests get worse, farmers find storing water more worthwhile, and those who can pay for it store more.
connections.simplification: Folds Relative attractiveness of storing water, which gathered the drivers of this decision: each driver now points at Freshwater storage measures itself, whose description says how farmers weigh storing against their other ways through a dry summer. The attractiveness raised the decision (+), so the link keeps the sign of the step into it and no loop through it changes; the attractiveness was no actor's decision of its own. What it leaves out: whether farmers want to store, apart from whether they can (Farmers' capacity to invest), is no variable on the drawing, only in the description.

connections.description: What a storage measure costs comes out of the money left to invest: its investment in the year it is built, and its upkeep and energy each year it runs. For the island's farms, from a drainage firm's quotes at 2021 prices, anti-salinisation drainage costs about €2,500 a hectare over a life of 15 years, and double drainage €6,000 a hectare to collect the water, with €12,500 to €25,000 for a pump to a basin and €1.80 to €4.00 per m³ for the basin (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 33–34); the creek-ridge infiltration system designed for a cluster of farms on the island's eastern creek ridges, €140,000 to €200,000, written off over about 15 years (p. 50). A year's running costs, figures the study takes from earlier studies, start at €50 for a weir (p. 19), while a creek-ridge infiltration system takes €1,440 in electricity alone (p. 20). The study finds the investment costs high, and for many farms too risky to bear alone (pp. 4–5). Within the year it is built.
The more harvest salt takes, the more a tolerant variety is worth against the current one, so the more farmers grow it, perhaps only past a threshold.
connections.simplification: Folds Relative attractiveness of salt-tolerant varieties, which gathered the drivers of this decision: each driver now points at Adoption of salt-tolerant varieties itself, whose description says that farmers weigh a tolerant variety against the one they grow now. The attractiveness raised the decision (+), so the link keeps the sign of the step into it and no loop through it changes; the attractiveness was no actor's decision of its own.

connections.description: Better tolerant varieties on the market make switching more worthwhile, so more farmers grow them.
connections.simplification: Folds Relative attractiveness of salt-tolerant varieties, which gathered the drivers of this decision: each driver now points at Adoption of salt-tolerant varieties itself, whose description says that farmers weigh a tolerant variety against the one they grow now. The attractiveness raised the decision (+), so the link keeps the sign of the step into it and no loop through it changes; the attractiveness was no actor's decision of its own.

connections.description: The more of the current crops' harvest salt takes, the more a new salt-tolerant crop is worth against them, so the more farmers grow it, but only past a threshold: Dutch farmers in salinised areas mostly hold back from saline agriculture unless salt severely hits their production (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 57). In interviews across the salinisation-prone provinces, Zeeland among them, salt in a field was largely invisible and seldom measured, a lower yield hard to put down to salt alone, and the damage not yet significant enough to make it urgent; it would take more dry summers like 2018 (Beauchampet, 2022, p. 216). Nearly all interviewees did not see halophytes as part of the answer, for lack of markets, the soils' intolerance of salt and the hand work they take (p. 221). In Zeeland most farmers still grow the common salt-sensitive crops (van den Burg et al., 2024, p. 6), and on the island the response a source shows is giving up a sensitive crop, sown onions (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 31), not taking up a new one. The shift the island's farmers do show is to a crop they already grow, from onions to cereals, which the source puts down to drought (Raat et al., 2026, p. 49); the island grows proportionally fewer potatoes and vegetables, mainly onions, and more cereals, which tolerate salt better, than Goeree-Overflakkee, which is connected to the main water system and so can take in fresh water (p. 34, which names no data source or year). Many of the interviewees across the provinces see research on the salt tolerance of cash crops, especially of cultivars already on the market, as contributing to resilience to salt (Beauchampet, 2022, p. 221). Years, as farmers come to see the damage over dry summers: a delay.
connections.simplification: Folds Relative attractiveness of new salt-tolerant crops, which gathered the drivers of this decision: each driver now points at Adoption of new salt-tolerant crops itself, whose description says that farmers weigh a new crop against their current crops. The attractiveness raised the decision (+), so the link keeps the sign of the step into it and no loop through it changes; the attractiveness was no actor's decision of its own. What it leaves out: whether farmers want to switch, apart from whether they can (Farmers' capacity to invest), is no variable on the drawing, only in the description. Folds Farmers' experience of damage, a stock that builds over dry summers, into this link's delay: farmers respond to the damage they come to notice, not to the state of the soil. Every loop through the link keeps its polarity and its mechanism, and the delay is kept; what it leaves out is how far what farmers notice differs from what salt takes.

connections.description: Assured offtake lowers the risk of a new crop, so more farmers grow it.

What it leaves out: whether farmers want to switch, apart from whether they can (Farmers' capacity to invest), is no variable on the drawing, only in the description.

connections.description: A better price after transport makes a new crop more worthwhile against the current crops, so more farmers grow it. In France, the prices of pulses are reported not high enough against major crops such as wheat, so more price incentives are needed for farmers to grow them, and most stakeholders want outlets of higher value (Magrini et al., 2018, p. 9); a specific incentive to farmers in 2010 doubled the area of pulses in its first year, and it fell back the next, downstream actors not particularly interested in them (Meynard et al., 2018, p. 10); in the Netherlands' salinising provinces, Zeeland among them, nearly all interviewees did not see halophytes as part of the answer, mostly for lack of markets, the soils' intolerance and the hand work they take (Beauchampet, 2022, p. 221). In the Netherlands, interviews on quinoa and seed potatoes on saline soil found the lack of economic benefits the main constraint on scaling them (de Wit et al., 2022, p. 276). The same interviews, conducted as a contribution to the EU's North Sea Region SalFar project, find Dutch quinoa grown under contract for one distributor, which buys a pre-agreed amount at a fixed price and manages supply according to demand, a dependency interviewees name as hampering its uptake (de Wit et al., 2022, pp. 266, 268, 277). Where a crop is sold this way and no other buyer competes, as none had for quinoa (p. 268), that means a better price raises the hectares only as far as the buyer contracts more. Within the year: the crop is chosen each season.

connections.description: Farmers who know how to grow and sell a new crop find it less risky, so more of them grow it.
