What it leaves out: whether farmers want to switch, apart from whether they can (Farmers' capacity to invest), is no variable on the drawing, only in the description.

connections.description: Growing a new crop, on their own fields or their neighbours', teaches farmers how.

What a switch costs comes out of the money left to invest, in the year a field changes crop. Switching tends to be costly, its investments weighed against the chance that the new crop pays more than the current one, a horticulture trade site writes (HortiDaily, 2014), and for Dutch arable farms the investments or the time needed to change their operations, among other things, leave little room to take on climate and biodiversity (Polman et al., 2026, p. 4). What a switch costs depends on the crop: quinoa is sown with standard equipment and harvested with a combine (van Loo, 2023, p. 75). No source read gives what a switch costs on the island. Within the year.
Stable demand makes investing in processing more worthwhile.
connections.simplification: Folds Attractiveness of processing new crops locally, which gathered the drivers of this decision: each driver now points at Local processing capacity for new crops itself, whose description says that buyers and processors weigh it against processing the crops elsewhere. The attractiveness raised the decision (+), so the link keeps the sign of the step into it and no loop through it changes; the attractiveness was no actor's decision of its own.

connections.description: A plant or chain nearby takes the harvest at less cost to move and store it, so more of the price reaches the farmer. In France, minor crops grown far from their processor cost much to collect for their volume, one cooperative building a linseed chain paid farmers a premium to deliver to its silo, and those without storage suited to small batches sold them fast, below the best price (Meynard et al., 2018, p. 7): the cost of moving and storing a harvest rises with distance and falls with volume wherever a chain runs, so the mechanism transfers. No source read gives what farmers on the island are paid. A plant that is large against the harvest within its reach can still pay less than the crop is worth to it: in Indiana, USA, where corn farmers pay the transport to the plant, a model estimates that transport cost, by softening competition from rival buyers, let plants pay on average 0.49 dollars a bushel (9% of the corn price) below the corn's value to them net of processing cost, and capacity running full added 0.18 dollars (Jung et al., 2022, pp. 614–616). Within the year: the price is set each season or contract.

Plants outside Zeeland are where the island's growers can sell a new crop now, at the plant's price less the haul: most Dutch quinoa growers have contracts with GreenFood50 (DutchNews.nl, 2026), based in Wageningen, which has its quinoa grown close to its processing facilities, to cut transport (GreenFood50, n.d.). That more processing elsewhere raises that price, by processors competing for the harvest or by a plant nearer the island, no source read shows. Within the year: the price is set each season or contract.

ask actors.for: How processors set the price they pay for new salt-tolerant crops, and whether a second buyer or a plant nearer the island raises it

connections.description: Growing the current crops year after year builds up know-how in growing, storing and selling them, and that know-how is of little use for a new crop.
connections.simplification: Folds Know-how of the current crops, a stock between the two: growing the current crops builds know-how, which is of little use for a new crop. The sign is the product of the two steps (+, then +), so no loop through the link changes, and know-how is no actor's decision. What one link leaves out: the know-how as a stock of its own, built up over years of growing the crops.

connections.description: The more a farm owns that only its current crops can use, the more a switch leaves idle: a store still stands when its crops take a smaller part of the rotation, and its costs do not fall (Polman et al., 2026, pp. 15, 17), and expensive machines are in some cases suited to one or a few crops (Bonnet & Tiktak, 2025, p. 45). What a new crop can use is not lost (Capital lost on switching). A machine or building can still earn after its crop leaves the farm when it is rented out or used for work for other farms: nationally, a relatively large share of arable farms with a standard output below 250,000 euro have other income, such as from renting out machines or buildings or from contract work (Bonnet & Tiktak, 2025, p. 36). The source does not say whether that work uses root-crop machines or stores, and a salinity shock that moves the island's farms off the same crops at once may shrink that work too, which no source read measures. Within the year, at the moment of switching.

What a farm's capital would stop earning holds it to its current crops. Of four arable farmers interviewed about a scheme for less intensive rotations, one, in the loess of Limburg, had recently built a store, which stands and which they want to use, and they and a farmer with plans for water storage said the investment has to be used, so that the onions stored, for example, would not soon leave the rotation (Dijkshoorn-Dekker et al., 2024, pp. 57, 71). Investments in expensive machines suited to one or a few crops keep a contractor and a farmer dependent on those crops for a long time (Bonnet & Tiktak, 2025, p. 45). It holds while the crops can be grown: in the island's low polders, where the surface water is salty all year, farmers have stopped growing sensitive crops such as sown onions (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 31). On the island as a whole the lack of fresh water seems to set the share: its one interviewed farmer, with half his rotation in root crops, judged the calculated move to a less intensive rotation relatively cheap to reach there "door zoetwatergebrek" (for lack of fresh water), and the workshop held high-margin crops no option on an island with little fresh water (Dijkshoorn-Dekker et al., 2024, pp. 56–57, 59). An exploration of the island by the water institute KWR sees a clear shift to less intensive crops in response to drought, fewer onions and more cereals, and relatively fewer potatoes and vegetables, mainly onions, than on Goeree-Overflakkee, which can take in fresh water from the main water system (Raat et al., 2026, pp. 34, 49). Within the year, as the rotation is chosen each season.
Money left to invest can go to carrying on: wells, irrigation, drains, a new harvester.

The more of the rotation is potatoes and onions, the more a farm spends on what they need: in farm accounts across the Netherlands from 2014 to 2022 a larger share of ware potatoes, seed potatoes, onions and winter carrots goes with significantly higher costs that no crop is charged with, buildings and machines among them, and storing these crops takes a store (Polman et al., 2026, pp. 5, 11, 15). The authors estimate the crops' effect with a random-effects model whose assumption they call very strong and probably untrue: they limit the bias with control variables, but call the results less reliable (Polman et al., 2026, pp. 5, 12–13). In France, specialising in a few crops is explained in part by writing off the equipment (Magrini et al., 2018, p. 3). The differences lie mostly between farms, less in how one farm changes over the years (Polman et al., 2026, p. 4): machines are written off at 8.2% a year and buildings at 3%, about 12 and 33 years if written off evenly (Janssens et al., 2020, p. 13). Years, so a delay.

What a farm spends on carrying on with its current crops is not left for other uses, in the year it is spent: the water board's general rule asks a horizontal well to pump fresh groundwater for irrigation (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026f, art. 2.9 lid 2 h), a horizontal well for brackish water cost €25,000 to €40,000 in a 2022 estimate (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 48–49), and irrigation systems cost relatively much to install, not always within a farmer's reach (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 28). Within the year.

Spending adds to this capital as far as it buys machines and stores for the current crops, not wells or drains: on Dutch arable farms the main category of investment is machines, implements and installations (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19, from national farm accounts), and a store for long keeping is a mostly insulated building with a cooling installation (Janssens et al., 2020, p. 5).

A farm pumps groundwater only through a well it has paid for: in Zeeland the water board's general rule lets a farm pump for irrigation of more than 10 m³ an hour, up to 60 m³ an hour, 3,000 m³ a quarter and 8,000 m³ a year, without a permit but notified at least four weeks ahead, through a horizontal well, from a fresh groundwater body its map shows outside its vulnerable areas, one at least 15 m thick or reaching the geohydrological base (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026f, arts. 1.1, 2.9 lid 2 h and 4.8 b and f); on the island's eastern creek ridges some farmers have laid a deep drain to take water from the ridge (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 38) and a livestock farmer irrigates from two (pp. 40, 43), and a horizontal well for brackish water cost €25,000 to €40,000 in a 2022 estimate (pp. 48–49). Within the year, once the well is in.
connections.simplification: Stands for the whole effect on pumping of a farm's dependence on its current crops, the direct link from Dependence on high-margin salt-sensitive crops folded into this chain: the high-value crops' need for water in a dry spell is in words here. The sign is the chain's (+, then +), so no loop changes its polarity. What it leaves out: a farm that already has wells can irrigate more of a thirsty crop within the year, while the chain runs through the delay on Dependence on high-margin salt-sensitive crops → Spending on keeping the current crops.

connections.description: A farm with less equity against its debt is a riskier loan: a high solvency can let a farm borrow more and at a lower rate (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19), and more financing still requires a contribution of the farm's own (Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, p. 3). Dutch banks assess investment plans by cash flows, solvency rates and the entrepreneur's track record (van der Meulen & van Asseldonk, 2017, p. 2), and a Rabobank adviser holds that a farm may be expected to have a solvency of at least 30 or 40% (Banken.nl, 2019). Banks weigh it beside the farm's cash flow, which counts more and more (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19). In a simulation of banks' check on 264 Dutch dairy farms, 2009–2017, with two criteria the author set (a new loan within the repayment capacity from past net cash flow, and solvency not below 30%), solvency was the limit for only 1.2% of farm observations, and the author holds that solvency rarely limits a bank loan because most Dutch dairy farms are rich in land, which gives banks the confidence that they will recover their finance even in default (Lamkowsky, 2023, pp. 51, 55–56, 94, 101). Dutch arable farms had on average a higher solvency still, 81% in 2018 against 74% on dairy farms, though it differs widely within each type (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 21), and the study calls its test conservative, as Dutch banks might have lent more thanks to dairy farms' high solvency (Lamkowsky, 2023, p. 60). Within the year: a bank judges it with each loan.

A public plan that may change what a farm can earn enters its bank's assessment before the plan is decided. After the government announced its nitrogen plans in June 2022 (Rabobank, 2025, p. 246), a significant part of Rabobank's loans to livestock farmers migrated to stage 2, where the bank places the exposures it considers to have a significant increase in credit risk, which it called also a reflection of the high level of uncertainty (Rabobank, 2023, p. 62); in 2024 it still held an adjustment of 23 million euro to its expected credit losses for the uncertainty the plans left, scoring livestock farmers on the profitability and sustainability of their business model (Rabobank, 2025, p. 246), and its lending criteria include a farm's nearness to a Natura 2000 area (p. 83). Measured for the nitrogen plans and livestock farms across the Netherlands; no source read shows a bank weighing a water level plan, and the mechanism transfers by the bank's test, whether the farm will keep earning enough to meet its obligations, which it applies to every farm loan (Farm income → Banks' risk assessment of farm loans). Within the year: the bank updates its vulnerable sectors at least every half-year (Rabobank, 2023, p. 62).

Banks lend less to farms they see as riskier: they have become more critical in lending, counting farm loans riskier despite the land as security (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 47), and hold back on investments not yet proven to pay (p. 8); Dutch farms' bank loans have fallen slightly in recent years, partly through the stricter rules (p. 19). Rabobank, which finances about 85% of Dutch farmers, says that since 2012, in a riskier world, it has often limited the level of financing on farms, and that a farm should be able to bridge two bad years without the bank (Banken.nl, 2019). Rabobank's outstanding agricultural loans fell by 4.3 billion euro between 2010 and 2018, to 26 billion euro, but largely because farmers asked for less credit amid uncertainty over future environmental and climate rules, the bank's stricter stance a further cause, so the fall does not measure this link alone (Banken.nl, 2019, the financial daily FD's calculation from Rabobank's annual reports, for the Netherlands as a whole and all farm types, on a news site that lists Rabobank as a partner). What the bank charges for the risk is Risk premium on farm loans. Within the year: a bank decides on a loan when it is asked.

Banks charge more for loans they see as riskier: the expected losses and the capital held against a loan, which the premium covers, rise with the credit risk the bank sees in the farm's creditworthiness, the size of the loan, its security and the sector's prospects (ABN AMRO, n.d.-a), and within the terms agreed a bank can change the premium during the loan when the farm's creditworthiness changes (n.d.-b). Where a bank judges a farm investment too risky it may also refuse the loan outright: 51% of the surveyed Dutch farms whose loan application was rejected (15% of medium- and long-term applications in 2017) named too high an investment risk as a reason, though banks put their rejection rate for farmers at 1–2%, and stakeholders interviewed say banks are more inclined to reject loan applications based on untested innovative ways of farming (fi-compass, 2020, pp. 17, 24, 33, a study made with EU funding, measured in a survey of 301 Dutch farms, not split by sector, on their 2017 applications). Within the year: the bank sets the premium with each loan and can revise it during the loan.

Credit is part of what a farm can invest: banks steering their lending more by cash flow can leave less room to invest in developing the farm and in sustainability (van der Meulen et al., 2020, pp. 47–48), and a farm short of cash, once savings and cuts fall short, can ask its bank to defer part of its interest and repayments or for more credit (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 28). The link has force mainly where a farm's own funds fall short: in an unbalanced panel of 264 Dutch dairy farms (accounts 2006–2017, measured on dairy, not arable, farms), the share that the model classified as financially constrained compared with their peers fell from 44% in 2009 to 8% in 2017, and a simulated stricter Basel IV lending scenario would have raised the share over the whole period only slightly, from 28.1% to 31.0% (Lamkowsky, 2023, pp. 44, 55, 57–58). Dutch farms in the fi-compass survey that did not apply for a loan in 2017 gave as main reason sufficient own funds (54.6%) or an earlier loan that already covered their needs (48.8%) (fi-compass, 2020, p. 22, the whole agriculture sector, not arable farms alone), while interviewed stakeholders place the hard access to bank finance with young farmers and new entrants, and the study adds farmers with untested ideas that banks see as too risky (p. 9). Within the year: credit granted is capacity at once.

A new loan adds to a farm's debt while its equity stays the same, so its debt rises relative to its assets and its solvency falls, solvency being its equity as a percentage of its total capital minus deferred tax (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19). Refinancing replaces a loan and adds no debt: the link counts the new money. Farms that expanded in recent years have a lower solvency (Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, p. 3); Dutch farmers under 45 had 68% in 2018 against 76% for those over 65, their higher long-term debt going partly with taking over the farm (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 26); on dairy farms heavy investment and poor results together took five points off solvency between 2006 and 2015 (Silvis et al., 2017, p. 2). The sign holds with the assets' value unchanged: the debt of Dutch arable farms rose 38% between 2010 and 2022, yet in 2022 it was 28% of their balance sheet, the smallest share in farming, as equity grows mainly through the rising value of the land (CBS, 2024). Less credit slows the debt's rise; the debt itself falls through repayments. Within the year: a loan is on the balance sheet once it is paid out.

More credit, more to pay each year: a farm's financing charges are the interest and commission on its loans and the repayment, the periodic amount that pays a loan back within the agreed term (ABN AMRO, n.d.-a), so each new loan adds its interest and repayment to what the farm pays. Within the year, from the loan's payout.

A higher premium raises the interest farms pay: a loan's rate changes when its specific premium does (ABN AMRO, n.d.-b), and the farms' operations often leave little or no room for higher financing costs (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 47). The bank sets the premium with each new loan and may revise it during a loan within its terms (ABN AMRO, n.d.-b), so the change reaches the payments as loans are made or revised: within the year, the source giving no timing. The banks' sector body's code of conduct bars a bank from changing a fixed rate during its fixed-rate period, or a premium agreed as fixed for a period, unless the client breaches its loan terms, while a variable premium may change, for example with a change in the client's risk profile (Nederlandse Vereniging van Banken, 2023, p. 15), so on a loan under the code with a fixed total rate or a fixed premium a higher premium reaches the payments only at the next reset, a new loan or a breach. These rules hold for loans requested from 1 July 2023, earlier loans from 1 July 2018 falling under the code's first version (p. 9), and for clients with a yearly group turnover up to 5 million euro and loans totalling up to 2 million euro (p. 5), a loan limit the average Dutch arable farm's bank loans of almost 1 million euro in 2018 stay within (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 21); no source read gives the island's farms' debt. No source read gives how much of the farms' debt carries a premium the bank can revise.

Interest is a cost that lowers a farm's income. Income is revenue less the costs paid and depreciation, plus extraordinary items (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 21), a definition that does not name repayments, yet the arable farms with a positive net cash flow, 55% in 2016, received enough to meet their payment obligations, repayments included, and 3% had a cash flow so low that they may not survive (p. 23): the link joins the two as one assumption, so that repayments reach what a farm can invest through its income, which keeps every loop's polarity.

A farm with high debt payments keeps its lucrative but salt-sensitive crops to meet them. No source read tests this, so its sign is the hypothesis's question: a farm with more debt may instead choose less risky crops.

With more bank credit more farmland is bought, and with less, less: the land a farm can acquire depends on its income and expected income together with its financing (Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, p. 2); with arable returns swinging, banks want larger buffers, which leave less room to finance land, and with a land loan calculated over at most 30 years with repayment, financing land has grown ever harder, which loosens the tie between owning land and using it, while younger farmers, by Rabobank's account, care less about expanding by purchase and are open to lease (pp. 3–4). The route the other way, a farm refused credit selling up, no source read shows: few Dutch farms go bankrupt, 45 in 2016, a large part of farm bankruptcies being in greenhouse horticulture, and a farm short of cash first saves on its spending or uses its savings, and only where that is not enough can ask its bank to defer part of its interest and repayments or for more credit, the bank weighing its continuity over the long term (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 28). Measured nationally. Within the year: a purchase follows its financing.

A farm without a successor is more likely to end when its farmer stops, its land then coming onto the market: over the long term the number of Dutch farms falls by 2 to 3% a year, mainly as farms end at the change of generation, the lack of a successor among the reasons, and the farmers who downsize or end their farm mainly set the supply of land (Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, p. 2). Measured nationally. The land changes hands as the farm ends.

Owners attached to their land keep it rather than sell it. In the Krimpenerwaard, the wish not to lose their land, from an emotional bond with it, was an important reason owners chose to turn it into nature themselves rather than sell it, and for one farm its bond with the land weighed more than moving (Kamphorst et al., 2025, pp. 11, 49, 68). Measured where a plan for nature, with expropriation as its last step, left owners only those choices; no source read measures it on the island's land market. Within the year: it acts when an owner decides whether to sell.

Expropriated land passes to the body that expropriates it when a notary's deed of expropriation is entered in the public registers (Omgevingswet, 2026, art. 11.18), which can be drawn up only once the expropriation order and the plan it carries out are irrevocable and the provisional compensation is paid (art. 11.16); on the island, the order for the high-voltage station takes effect only once the court has confirmed it (Gemeente Schouwen-Duiveland, 2026, p. 1). Years, so a delay: in the Krimpenerwaard, under the law before the Omgevingswet, the order of October 2020 left two years before the owners still without an agreement had to be summoned to court, by October 2022 (Kamphorst et al., 2025, pp. 26, 45), and the process of the owners expropriated by the court ran more than 61 months on average (p. 67), with continued use of the land until it was handed over (p. 41).
Land that changes hands leaves arable farming when its next holder does not farm it.

Where arable farming still pays, its holder, present or next, keeps the land arable, while what arable farming earns, not what other uses would bid, sets the land's price. A decade or more: land leaves arable use only when a holder gives it up, and just over 1.5% of Zeeland's farmland is sold in a year (Agricultural land value).

Arable land needs lower ditch levels than grassland or nature. By the water board's rules for its whole area, a water level plan starts from an optimal level for each use and soil, the farmland's derived from the optimal drain depths for farming: for arable farming and horticulture 120 cm below the surface on salt-marsh clay (schorgronden) with no sand within 1.2 m, down to 60 on peat, for permanent grassland as a rule 20 cm less (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 7, 19), and for nature 0 cm as a general starting point, its levels set with the site managers, as Duiveland's analysis applied them to its land-use map of 2018 (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, pp. 16–17, 29). So the more hectares farmed as arable land, the more land whose farmers need low levels, in spring as their soil work allows (2021a, p. 66); how strongly they ask for them, no source read shows (Farmers' demand for deep polder drainage → Water board's plans to raise ditch levels). Within the year: the need goes with the land's use each season, while the land leaves arable use only as it changes hands (Arable land in the polders).
A farm that pays finds a successor more easily.

A draft plan that would leave a field with less drainage depth than its use needs gives its owner reason to expect the land to earn less and so be worth less, before any level changes, and owners concerned that a plan lowers their land's value object to it and ask to be compensated; what the level itself does once it takes effect runs, years later, through Polder drainage depth and Spring workability of the fields to Agricultural land value. Respondents to Friesland's peat meadow programme said the uncertainty it creates for a farm's future value lowers the value of land and buildings before the programme takes effect, the 'planological shadow' (Provincie Fryslân & Wetterskip Fryslân, 2021, pp. 3, 31). In their views on draft level plans owners named that fall: in two peat polders, holding the water board liable or asking for a compensation scheme (Graas, 2021, pp. 5, 24), and calling a plan unacceptable because its burden fell on the farmers, in the value of their land and buildings among others (Hoogheemraadschap van Schieland en de Krimpenerwaard, 2022, pp. 5, 16–17), and in the Tielerwaard, on a raise beside a Natura 2000 area, the whole farm's as already at issue once the buffer zone was set (Waterschap Rivierenland, 2019, zienswijze 09). A water board compensates only damage beyond the normal societal risk, the rest staying, wholly or partly, with the owner (Hoogheemraadschap van Schieland en de Krimpenerwaard, 2022, p. 16; Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 14). Whether and how far land loses value the minister called unclear for the peat meadow areas, the question being whether the yield can stay the same or the farmer can earn a comparable income on the land another way (Minister van Landbouw, Natuur en Voedselkwaliteit, 2021, pp. 2–3). Measured elsewhere, in polders where the level change answers subsidence; it transfers as an owner's response to a plan that would leave a field too wet for its use, as in the Braakman near Terneuzen in 2015, where the island's own water board answered ZLTO, objecting for seven farmers, that some would be left with less than optimal drainage depth or with drains under water in winter, both naming damage, not the land's value (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2015, p. 2). On the island the raises of 2021 were to limit drought damage and give the crops more moisture (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 69; 2021b, p. 53): no view on either plan, as the board summarises them, gave the land's value as a reason, the only ones against a raise naming flooding in extreme rain (2021a, p. 53), as farmers across the salinisation-prone provinces want their levels low against flooding and to work their fields with heavy machinery (Beauchampet, 2022, p. 217), and one submitter on each half asked about holding a higher level locally (2021a, p. 53; 2021b, p. 7). Whether a raise that leaves too little drainage depth would raise this concern on the island, no source read shows, nor objections on this ground to the other bodies' plans. In its own rule for its own plans, the island's water board says damage from a deliberate change of a field's drainage depth, as a raise is, is usually not seen as natural and is likely to have to be compensated, where possible by technical measures or by buying or exchanging land (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 15). Within the year: the views come in the six weeks a draft lies open (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 17).
connections.simplification: Folds Owners' concern about their land's value, which gathered the reasons for objecting: a fall in the land's value, and a plan that would lower it, raised landowning farmers' concern, and the concern raised their objections. The sign is the product of the two steps, so B13 keeps its polarity, and the concern was no actor's decision of its own. A tenant's concern, losing the lease, was never part of it. What it leaves out: why owners object is no variable on the drawing, a question for the group model building session.

connections.description: Farmers who expect public bodies to keep their commitments object less. In views on draft water plans in peat areas, owners named unreliable government, a hidden agenda and agreements not kept beside their other grounds (Graas, 2021, p. 13; Provincie Fryslân & Wetterskip Fryslân, 2021, pp. 6, 14, 85; Hoogheemraadschap van Schieland en de Krimpenerwaard, 2022, p. 29). In an experiment with students in Leiden, on a board advising the national government on carbon dioxide storage, how trustworthy the decision maker seemed explained how far they accepted the decision (Terwel, 2009, pp. 77–78, 81), and in the United States distrust of risk managers goes with political activism (Slovic, 1993, pp. 675–676). Measured elsewhere; it transfers as an owner's response to a body that plans for their land, whatever the plan's reason. That transfer gives a direction, not a strength: Terwel's participants were not personally involved in the decision making, and their own attitude to carbon dioxide storage did not change how far they accepted the advice (Terwel, 2009, pp. 80–82), whereas a farmer objecting to a plan for their own fields may judge it on their own view of it. It holds while a farmer still acts on the distrust: a view in Friesland reports 'weinig vertrouwen en veel gelatenheid' (Provincie Fryslân & Wetterskip Fryslân, 2021, p. 7), and one submission has a small group on the island, no longer trusting the Province, starting a pipeline plan of its own (Lases, 2021, p. 2). None of the views on the island's two level plans of 2021, as the board summarises them, named trust (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 53; 2021b, pp. 7–8). Within the year: the views come in the six weeks a draft lies open (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 17).
Farmers attached to their land resist plans for it beyond what it is worth in money.

Hypothesis, with two mechanisms for the group model building session: the conflict over a plan itself may lower trust, and a plan delayed, changed or dropped after objections may teach farmers not to count on the next one. Farmers do name changing plans as a reason to distrust public bodies (Farmers' trust in government), but no source read shows a plan changed because of objections costing trust, and where a body takes up an objection those who objected may trust it more: farmers feel their input is ignored, which the Ombudsman concludes leads to distrust (Farmers' trust in government), but no source read shows input taken up raising trust, so the sign is part of the question. Within the year once a plan changes: trust can be destroyed in an instant; its recovery, slower, is in the element.
connections.simplification: Folds Plans changed or dropped. The sign is the product of the two steps (+, then −), so no loop through the link changes. It assumes that a plan changed after objections costs trust as a plan changed for other reasons does, which no source read shows. The public bodies' decisions on their plans stay drawn, on the links from Objections to land-use plans into Water board's plans to raise ditch levels and Farmland planned for other uses.

connections.description: Land taken against its owner's wish lowers how far farmers expect public bodies to keep their commitments, the more so where they do not count the purpose as a public interest and where voluntary purchase was promised. Of 14 owners interviewed in the Krimpenerwaard, in a process of 2015–2023 with expropriation for nature as its last step, most experienced it as negative, and they often named an inequality of power; the municipal council had feared for trust between government and farming (Kamphorst et al., 2025, pp. 10, 15, 55). In interviews in the Netherlands, owners who did not count the plan as a public interest, nature development for one, were more often negative about expropriation in itself than those who did, as for roads (Holtslag-Broekhof et al., 2016, p. 180), and the chair of LTO held large-scale use against reliable government, farmers having been told that purchases would be voluntary (Neefjes, 2008, p. 3). The pressure starts before any order: the possibility of one weighs heavily on the process and on the owners' lives (Kamphorst et al., 2025, p. 55). No source read measures trust before and after, or on the island, where the purposes used so far are a road and the grid, those owners accept most. A tenant may gain (Adviescommissie Natuurherstel Westerschelde, n.d., p. 11). How negatively owners judge an expropriation afterwards seems to depend on its outcome and process: in the same Krimpenerwaard evaluation, paid for by the Province and municipality that ran the process and by the agriculture ministry, most of the owners interviewed were satisfied with their end situation, though half of those who sold rather than make the nature themselves were very dissatisfied, and satisfaction with the end result regularly contributed to a milder judgement of the whole process afterwards (Kamphorst et al., 2025, pp. 9, 13, 53), and Holtslag-Broekhof et al. (2016, p. 183) conclude that expropriation need not be feared in itself where its public purpose is clearly communicated, the process is open and takes owners' interests seriously, and the owner ends in the same economic position as before. Within the year: trust can be destroyed in an instant, its recovery, slower, is in the element (Slovic, 1993, p. 677).
Objections delay, change or stop a plan in which the municipality designates farmland for another use, while it is pending; with none pending, they change nothing.
A plan that designates farmland for another use leads its owners and the farmers who work it to object, appeal and lobby against it.

Farmland the plan designates for another use leaves arable farming as the plan is carried out on it: the plan does not end the farming by itself. In the Krimpenerwaard, where the land-use plan designating farmland for nature became irrevocable in October 2021 (Kamphorst et al., 2025, p. 25), of the land of owners who settled by agreement without converting it themselves most was sold to the province, 152 hectares, or exchanged, 59 (p. 41), and 24 agreements were made for owners to turn land into nature themselves, on 171 hectares of their own and 274 leased from the province (p. 67), the largest area (p. 41), an amicable purchase or exchange being the most common outcome, closely followed by the owners' own conversion (p. 36); voluntary sale and the owners' own conversion alone had not completed it in earlier periods (p. 10). Years, so a delay: the sales took more than 30 months on average, the owners' own conversion more than 61 (p. 67). Expropriation is drawn apart (Farmland planned for other uses → Expropriation of farmland). Measured for nature in the peat meadows of South Holland; the procedure is national law, and how long it takes on the island no source read gives.

More winter rain soaks deep into the dunes and the sandy creek ridges, where the winter's rain surplus refills the lens (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3661, 3673, 3675, measured on the island; van Beekom et al., 1953a, p. 155, for the Netherlands). Years, so a delay: the lens is a Stock.

A notification renewed after a lapsed one, the well not built within two years, is judged on the rules and the fresh groundwater bodies established at that moment (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b, the explanation of art. 2.9), and the rules in force let a farm pump for irrigation of more than 10 m³ an hour, up to 60 m³ an hour, 3,000 m³ a quarter and 8,000 m³ a year, without a permit but notified at least four weeks ahead, from a fresh groundwater body the board's map shows outside its vulnerable areas, one at least 15 m thick or reaching the geohydrological base (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026f, arts. 1.1 and 4.8 b and f), so the thicker the lens, the more pumping the rules allow. The rules allow the same 800 m³ per hectare a year on any fresh groundwater body the board's map shows outside its vulnerable areas, one of 15 m or more or one reaching the geohydrological base, so a lens the map shows there may be pumped without a permit, under the general rules and within 8,000 m³ a year, 3,000 m³ a quarter and 60 m³ an hour per extraction, but one thickening beyond it adds none (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026f, arts. 1.1, 2.9 and 4.8). The map of fresh bodies is revised periodically, and wells in use that a revision leaves outside them may still be used while new ones are no longer allowed (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2019, p. 20, the water board's own policy note), so a thinning lens lowers the allowance once a revision leaves it outside the fresh bodies; whether the rules in force still hold that is unclear, since outside the fresh bodies and the vulnerable areas they free from a permit an extraction with a pump of more than 5 m³ an hour or of at most 12,000 m³ a year, whatever it is for (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026f, art. 4.8 e). Apart from any revision, the board can forbid an extraction that harms, or threatens to harm, the interests of groundwater management (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b, art. 2.9 lid 4). No delay: no source read shows how often those bodies are updated.
connections.simplification: The link reads the rules in force as letting a lens be pumped without a permit only where the board's map shows a fresh body, as the water board's 2019 policy note says; the regulation's art. 4.8 e, as written, frees outside the fresh bodies too an extraction with a pump of more than 5 m³ an hour or of at most 12,000 m³ a year, while art. 4.9 frees from notification a pump of not more than 5 m³ an hour, which suggests a drafting error (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026f, arts. 4.8 e and 4.9). Which reading the board applies is a question for the water board.

connections.description: The board has the chloride in the pumped water measured every 2 to 3 years and can forbid pumping that harms the groundwater (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b, art. 2.9, paragraphs 2f and 4). Years, so a delay: the measuring interval.

Farmers pump within what the rules allow: pumping that fails a condition is forbidden (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b, art. 2.9, paragraph 7). Whether farms keep to it rests on their own records: the rule has them meter or time their pumping and report the volume yearly (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b, art. 2.9, paragraph 2 c and g), and the water board wrote in 2019 that these self-reported yearly returns make it hard to check in the field whether everyone keeps to the maxima, and that, with its register of wells out of date, landowners are more likely to build wells at unsuitable locations without contacting it (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2019, pp. 21–22, the board on its own enforcement). Within the year.

Double drainage would collect fresh drain water into a basin, from which a farm could irrigate that season, a system that works in concept but has not yet been tested in practice (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 23, 29, 32–33, for the island). What the other measures keep reaches crops through the lenses. Within the year.

Many farmers on the island say they want to invest in holding fresh water and hold back while how a measure works there, what it costs, risks and yields stay uncertain (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 4, 11); they are readier to invest in a solution shown to work in practice somewhere (p. 56). What is learned can also rule a measure out where a farm's ground does not suit it: the feasibility studies in the island's low polders find the deep groundwater west of the creek ridge too saline to store fresh water in, making basins above ground the most feasible storage (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 32), and anti-salinisation drainage hydrologically feasible only with light seepage and a fairly permeable subsoil, at 2 of 5 locations (p. 33). On the test strips at Kerkwerve, on the island, the effect of anti-salinisation drainage seems limited, probably through poorly permeable unripened clay, a high ditch level and old shallow drains left largely working (Oude Essink et al., 2018, p. 97), though the trial's own report, Deltares and Acacia having run it (p. 73), sees indications that it would work under better conditions (pp. 97–98). How long this takes, no source read shows.

Where farms do not invest in measures, the techniques are not refined or adapted, nothing is learned from building them and their effects cannot be monitored, so no knowledge base forms at agricultural advisers and contractors (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 11–12). One measure built and monitored on the island taught what limited it, but left uncertain whether it freshened the rainwater lens: at the Drains2Buffer trial at Kerkwerve, built in 2013, a ditch level 10–40 cm above the deep drains' outlet limited them, while the measuring plots had freshened for a reason other than the measure, discovered only on the last measuring day (Oude Essink et al., 2018, pp. 73, 96–97, the trial researchers' own report). The farmer must also gain experience operating controlled drainage, and in a 2009 survey the systems laid in Zeeland at the end of 2008 had, partly because 2009 was dry, given no experience of storing water yet (Stuyt et al., 2012, p. 51, four farms in Zeeland, for STOWA, the regional water managers' knowledge centre). How long this takes, no source read shows.

Hypothesis: storing water is a long investment that a change of rules can strand, so the less farmers expect public bodies to keep their commitments on water and land, the less they store. A question for the group model building session.

The board tests each level area's drainage depth against the optimum for its use and soil: where more than 10% of the area is too wet, 10 cm or more short of the optimum, the target level is to be lowered or the discharge's bottlenecks solved, and where less than 10% is, a raise is considered (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 9). On Duiveland four level areas may run a lower target for a while in wet periods, where the fields' drainage and workability need it (2021a, p. 40). The test sets a criterion only for the share too wet; for the share too dry it sets none, only an aim to keep it small (2025, pp. 9–10; 2021b, p. 37), and Schouwen's study read more than 25% too dry in summer only as a sign the levels may be too low (2021b, p. 44), so a deep drainage depth need not start a raise. On Schouwen 37 of 43 sub-level areas, 85% of the area tested, were more than half too dry in winter and 31, 48% of it, in summer, the season that weighs more, while those holding 62% of it were more than 10% too wet in summer, partly because levels are held high there on purpose against peat compaction, and the board judged the level right in most of the area and proposed a raise in ten level areas, in two by more than 10 cm (2021b, pp. 37, 44–45, 53–54; the board's own report on its own plan). Years, so a delay: the test runs as a plan is prepared, which the board does when its evaluation every three years finds a plan no longer current, or once a plan is 17 years old (2025, pp. 16–17).

By the water board's rules the level follows the land's use ("peil volgt functie"): the board adapts it to what an area needs (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 5), reading the use from the current land use and from the uses the municipality's land-use plan designates, with what is expected within about five years (p. 7). A plan starts from the optimal level for each use and soil, nature's set with the site managers (2021a, p. 29), and where nature and farmland share a level area on Duiveland the plan keeps nature's level and keeps the farm parcel draining, in one area by linking it to the neighbouring, lower area, in the other by closing a leak (2021a, pp. 61–62). So the less land is farmed as arable land, the more reason for a raise, whoever asks. By the board's own study for its plan, in most of Duiveland's level areas a raise is possible only once the discharge capacity is enlarged, since levels in several are kept low on purpose to store extreme rain (2021a, p. 69), and the province's norm for that storage and discharge capacity, which the board tests against, is the same once in 25 years for arable land and grassland (2021a, pp. 12, 33–34; Provincie Zeeland, 2024, art. 3.3, p. 2), so land that goes from arable crops to grass is held to the same norm as before. In 2026 the board proposed to enlarge Duiveland's discharge capacity against flooding, and its slides give no date (2026a, slides 12, 17), though the province asks the board, as a duty of effort, to meet the norm by 1 January 2028 (Provincie Zeeland, 2024, art. 3.3, p. 2), so whether the limit lifts before 2050 is open. Years, so a delay: the board weighs it as it prepares a plan, which it does when its evaluation every three years finds a plan no longer current, or once a plan is 17 years old (2025, pp. 16–17).

The saltier the field, the fewer of the crops most sensitive to salt a farm keeps: on low fields with strong saline seepage on the island, farmers have stopped growing sensitive crops such as sown onions (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 31). Years, so a delay: salt in a field is largely invisible and seldom measured, a lower yield is hard to put down to it, and interviewees expected it to take more dry summers like 2018 to make salt urgent (Beauchampet, 2022, p. 216, interviews in the salinisation-prone provinces, Zeeland among them).
connections.simplification: Folds Farmers' experience of damage, a stock that builds over dry summers, into this link's delay: farmers respond to the damage they come to notice, not to the state of the soil. Every loop through the link keeps its polarity and its mechanism, and the delay is kept; what it leaves out is how far what farmers notice differs from what the soil shows.

connections.description: With more fresh water a farm may keep or take on the crops that need it: on the island's low polders, with more fresh water available the farmer is open to more profitable crops, a more varied rotation, or both (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 30). In Zeeland the area of sown onions halved from 4,705 ha in 2019 to 2,579 ha in 2024, the article naming the dry summers, the poor harvests and the lack of fresh water, four in five arable farmers having none, as farmers preferred less risky crops, while elsewhere the area grew (De Vriend, 2024b, for Zeeland). Years, so a delay: farmers respond to the seasons they have had, and the fall ran over five years of dry summers.
connections.simplification: Folds Farmers' experience of damage, a stock that builds over dry summers, into this link's delay: farmers respond to the damage they come to notice, not to the state of the soil. Every loop through the link keeps its polarity and its mechanism, and the delay is kept; what it leaves out is how far what farmers notice differs from what the soil shows.

connections.description: The margin given up is net of what the new crop earns, a margin being revenue minus the crop's variable costs (Cloet et al., 2024, p. 1), so the better a new crop pays the less a farm gives up on each hectare it moves to it. Quinoa, in a study for Flanders, yields about 3 tonnes a hectare, sold at €1,100 a tonne under contract on a market still very small (pp. 2–3). Within the year: the crop is chosen each season.

Banks look more and more at a farm's cash flow, whether its operations earn enough to meet all its financial obligations (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19): the bank judges whether the farmer can generate enough over the longer term for interest and repayment, the expected income being the limiting factor rather than the size of the farm (Farjon et al., 2013, section Financiering van bedrijfsuitbreiding). Basel IV steers banks further toward profitability and liquidity rather than the value of collateral (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 47). So the less a farm earns, the more risk its bank sees, for owner and tenant alike; for the Netherlands. Within the year.

A public body can expropriate only for a use made possible in an adopted plan, a permit or a project decision (Omgevingswet, 2026, art. 11.6), and only after a reasonable attempt to buy has failed (art. 11.7), so the more farmland planned for other uses, the more farmland within reach of an order. Only part of it comes within reach: the need to expropriate lapses where the owner shows they are willing and able to realise the planned use themselves, has concrete plans for it made known to the authority, and will realise it in the way the authority intends (art. 11.7(2)), and land the legger lists as a bergingsgebied can stay with its owner, who must tolerate flooding and the temporary storage of surface water on it (art. 10.3(4); annex, bergingsgebied). Of 481 ha inside and outside the nature boundary in the 69 files studied, 24 owners agreed to realise nature on 171 ha of their own land and 92 ha went through the court (Kamphorst et al., 2025, pp. 10–11, measured in the Krimpenerwaard, a Zuid-Holland peat polder, in an evaluation commissioned by the Programmabureau Veenweiden Krimpenerwaard that ran it with the Province, and funded by the Province of Zuid-Holland, the municipality and the agriculture ministry). Years, so a delay: the attempt to buy and the order follow the adopted plan.

Summers with less rain and more evaporation lower the year's rain surplus, which is what refills the lens, so the lens thins. The rain surplus falls mostly in winter, since in summer by far most of the moisture evaporates (van Beekom et al., 1953a, p. 155, for the Netherlands). In a model of a drained field over saline seepage, built from measurements on the island, the recharge is each day's rain minus evaporation: in the year it used, summer evaporation (440 mm) outweighed summer rain (425 mm), so the winter did the recharging, and a smaller surplus gave a thinner lens (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3665, 3671, 3674). Model calculations show that higher summer evaporation shrinks the lens (de Louw et al., 2015, p. 12, in an article on the island's seepage fields, by researchers who then present Drains2buffer, a drainage design developed in the GO-FRESH project, as a way to grow the lens). Years, so a delay: the lens is a Stock that a year's recharge barely moves. In a model of a drained field over saline seepage, built from measurements on the island, the centre of the mixing zone moves at most 0.1 m in a year as the recharge swings with the seasons, the vertical flow at most 1.2 mm a day, and every run settled from saline groundwater to a stationary lens within 30 years (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3665, 3673), so a change in recharge takes years to show in the lens.

connections.description: More winter rain raises the winter's rain surplus, which soaks in and refills the lens. In a model of a drained field over saline seepage, built from measurements on the island, the recharge is each day's rain minus evaporation, and from October to March of the year it used 397 mm of rain fell against 108 mm of evaporation (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3665). Kaandorp et al. (2022, p. 11) expect the changing rain to raise the island's winter groundwater levels in part. The drains cap how much of a wetter winter reaches the lens: model calculations show that the extra winter water of wetter winters leaves through the intensive tile drainage and does not feed the lens (de Louw et al., 2015, p. 12, in an article on the island's seepage fields, by researchers who then present Drains2buffer, a drainage design developed in the GO-FRESH project, as a way to grow the lens); that part is drawn as Wetter winters -> Winter rain drained away. connections.description: Rain refills the lens only once it has soaked into the soil. Before the floods, Zeeland's well-drained clay let the winter's rain surplus soak through almost completely; once sodium had broken down the structure of the topsoil, it became impervious and sticky when wet, part of the rain ran off over the surface and pools stood on the land, the more so the heavier the clay (van Beekom et al., 1953a, p. 157; 1953b, pp. 230, 233, 236, measured in the flooded polders of Zeeland, by R1's own mechanism). Even so, in most of the well-drained soils at least 150 mm still seeped through in winter, and less in badly drained soils of low permeability, against a Dutch annual rain surplus of about 200 mm, most of it in winter (van Beekom et al., 1953a, pp. 155, 157). In model computations of wetter winters, the extra winter water drained off effectively through the intensive drainage without feeding the thin rain lenses of the saline seepage areas the authors studied in Zeeland, among them a tile-drained field on the island, so more rain soaking in may add little to the lens (de Louw et al., 2015, pp. 6, 11, 12, by authors who report on the GO-FRESH project, which developed a drainage system to grow the lens). The structure a soil has in a winter sets how much of that winter's rain soaks in, within the year; the slowness sits in the lens. Years, so a delay: the lens is a Stock that a year's recharge barely moves. In a model of a drained field over saline seepage, built from measurements on the island, the centre of the mixing zone moves at most 0.1 m in a year as the recharge swings with the seasons, the vertical flow at most 1.2 mm a day, and every run settled from saline groundwater to a stationary lens within 30 years (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3665, 3673), so a change in recharge takes years to show in the lens. How thick a lens the recharge builds is also set by the drainage depth and the seepage (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3674).

R1 runs through it: Root zone salinity -(-, delay)-> Soil structure -(+, delay)-> Rainwater lens thickness -(-)-> Root zone salinity, two minus signs, reinforcing as before, and its mechanism, salty soil taking in less rain so the lens thins over years, is this link's description.

connections.description: Rain the drains carry off does not refill the lens, so the lens thins: tile drains usually discharge shallow groundwater rapidly during rain, as other studies found (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3661), and model calculations show that the extra winter water leaves through the intensive tile drainage and does not feed the lens (de Louw et al., 2015, p. 12). On Schouwen-Duiveland upward saline seepage keeps the recharge within the clay and peat top layer of the low polders (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3662, 3674–3675), and recharge, seepage and drainage depth together set the lens's thickness, by measurements on the island and a model built from them (pp. 3662, 3673–3675). In a conceptual 2-D model of a tile-drained field with saline seepage, built from field measurements in Zeeland and a 3-D model of a field on the island, how readily the drains run (a drainage resistance of 0.5 to 7.5 days) changed the lens's depth and width by less than 0.1 m; across the model's parameters the lens's depth moved more between the drains than at them, where the centre of the mixing zone stayed within 0.1 m of drain depth (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3662, 3664–3666, 3671). The rain drained away follows each rain within the year; the slowness sits in the lens. Years, so a delay: the lens is a Stock that a year's recharge barely moves. In a model of a drained field over saline seepage, built from measurements on the island, the centre of the mixing zone moves at most 0.1 m in a year as the recharge swings with the seasons, the vertical flow at most 1.2 mm a day, and every run settled from saline groundwater to a stationary lens within 30 years (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3665, 3673), so a change in recharge takes years to show in the lens. The drains cap how much of a wetter winter reaches the lens: model calculations show that the extra winter water of wetter winters leaves through the intensive tile drainage and does not feed the lens (de Louw et al., 2015, p. 12, in an article on the island's seepage fields, by researchers who then present Drains2buffer, a drainage design developed in the GO-FRESH project, as a way to grow the lens).

Recharge is no actor's decision: the decisions that reach it, the farmers' storage measures and the water board's ditch levels, act on Winter rain drained away, which stays drawn, so no decision leaves the drawing. B6 and R4 run through it, with every other loop through the chain: Freshwater storage measures -(-)-> Winter rain drained away -(-, delay)-> Rainwater lens thickness keeps the farmers' storage acting on the lens by the rain kept in the field, B6 balancing and R4 reinforcing as before. It carries the drains' effect on the lens only through the rain they carry off. In de Louw et al.'s (2011, pp. 3664–3665) conceptual 2-D model of a tile-drained field, built from the island's field data, the depth of the tile drains also sets the lens's base (p. 3671, Fig. 12d). At a drain, the centre of the mixing zone stays within 0.1 m of the drain depth. Deeper drains give a deeper mixing zone, at and between the drains, so a thicker lens (pp. 3671, 3674, Fig. 12d). At the field's centre, the ditch's water level moved the lens by no more than 0.1 m (pp. 3665, 3671; Table 2 on p. 3666). So Polder drainage depth, the ditch level, needs no link of its own to the lens. The farms' drains are no variable. The measures that change them, controlled and anti-salinisation drainage, are counted in Freshwater storage measures, which keep the thin rainwater lens against salt (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 29). That is the sign the drawn path through Winter rain drained away gives, so B6 and R4 keep their polarity.

connections.description: The deeper the ditch levels lie below the fields, the more peat lies above the groundwater, where it compacts and oxidises, so the land surface falls faster relative to NAP: by the water board's rules for its whole area, peat soil above the groundwater subsides in response to drainage, and where the soil is prone to settling the board changes levels with restraint to limit it (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 13). The island's low polders lie on peat: in Schouwen's low polder salt-marsh soils alternate with basin clay with peat (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, p. 23), and under Duiveland a peat layer lies almost everywhere at −1.6 to −3.4 m NAP, under calcareous sand or light clay (2021a, p. 20), often within a metre of the surface in its low south and middle (p. 19); drained by ditches, the polders have sunk over several hundred years as the peat compacted and the clay ripened (2021b, pp. 20, 22; 2021a, p. 18). On the island the board holds Schouwen's summer levels high on purpose to limit subsidence by peat compaction, which leaves the salt-marsh soils between too little drainage depth (2021b, p. 45), and changes a level in soil prone to settling by no more than the land has subsided since (p. 50); Duiveland's plan changed levels with great care where peat lies below (2021a, p. 67). The rate of the fall follows the drainage within the year (the board weighs the risk by the summer groundwater level against the ditch level and the depth of the peat, 2021b, p. 50); the delay sits in the elevation, which the fall lowers at millimetres a year, so a decimetre takes decades: Dutch land below sea level is still subsiding up to 1 m per century, fastest in peat areas (Oude Essink et al., 2010, pp. 1, 3, 8–9). No source read gives how much faster the land falls per decimetre of drainage, nor a rate for Schouwen-Duiveland's clay polders.
connections.simplification: Folds Land subsidence, the rate at which the polders' surface falls, into the link: the sign is the product of the two steps (+, then −), so no loop through the link changes R or B, and each keeps its mechanism, drained peat compacting and oxidising and the land falling. The rate follows the drainage within the year and is no actor's decision; its slowness lies in the elevation, a Stock, which stays drawn, so the delay sits on this link. The link also holds the rate's response to the drainage as if the peat above the groundwater lasted to 2050: its organic matter oxidises as it is drained, which uses it up, but no source read gives how much peat is left on the island or how long it lasts. Drawn, the dwindling peat would only weaken the link, in a balancing loop of its own, never reverse it, so every loop through it keeps its polarity and its mechanism. The link also counts the drainage depth and the fall of the land as totals for the island, though how fast drainage makes the land fall differs by area with where peat lies above the groundwater: in Schouwen's low polder salt-marsh soils alternate with basin clay with peat (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, p. 23), and under Duiveland the peat lies often within a metre of the surface in its low south and middle (2021a, p. 19), so one level does not suit every soil: on Schouwen the board holds the summer levels high for the peat, which leaves the salt-marsh soils between too little drainage depth (2021b, p. 45). Deeper drainage lowers the land wherever it acts, so the link stays − and every loop through it keeps its polarity, and those loops run on through the seepage of the low polders, where the peat lies, so they keep their mechanism. What it leaves out: how strong the link is per area, which no source read gives for the island.

ask actors.for: How fast the island's polders subside, per area: the board changes a level in soil prone to settling by no more than the land has subsided since (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, p. 50).

connections.description: More hectares of new crops on the island give more harvest within reach of a processor or trader on or near the island, and that volume draws capacity. Quinoa has been grown in Zeeland since 2016, on one to four parcels a year at six locations in all (Bogers et al., 2025, pp. 28, 38), its map showing one of them on the island. Quinoa yields about 2,000 kg a hectare on average in Europe (van Loo, 2023, p. 79), and its yield varies from under 500 to over 4,000 kg (p. 76), harvested in the Netherlands in August of the year it is sown (p. 75). More harvest within reach makes a plant or chain nearby more worthwhile, so buyers and processors build or keep capacity on or near the island rather than handle the crops elsewhere. In France, the firms that store, process and sell crops specialised in a few dominant ones for economies of scale, and their logistics are not adapted to sorting pulses out of mixed crops (Magrini et al., 2018, pp. 3, 9), and a small volume spread out or far from its users costs more to collect and to source (Meynard et al., 2018, pp. 7–8): the economies of scale hold wherever a chain is built, so the mechanism transfers. In the Netherlands, on Terschelling's saline field, producers of processed products are more concerned about volumes than the restaurants are, and stakeholders describe a chicken and egg: a producer needs a market, and a reliable market needs ample supply (ten Dam et al., 2023, pp. 10, 14); for quinoa, one expert says efforts only work with concentrated investments and high volumes (de Wit et al., 2022, p. 270). Years: a Zeeland quinoa chain was a project from 2021 to 2024 (De Vriend, 2024a): the delay sits in building the chain, not in the harvest, which follows within the year.

It was an auxiliary no actor decides, with one link out; both steps into it are + and its link out is +, so each folded link is + and keeps the delay of building the chain. R7 runs Adoption of new salt-tolerant crops (+, delay) Local processing capacity for new crops (+) Net price for new crops after transport (+) Adoption: reinforcing as before, on the same mechanism, volume within reach drawing a chain nearby that cuts transport; every other loop through the harvest runs through this link too and keeps its sign. The harvest within reach counts every new crop as one volume, although its crops go to separate chains: quinoa to buyers such as GreenFood50 (DutchNews.nl, 2026), samphire to a Zeeland trader in sea vegetables (FreshPlaza, 2018); read per crop, the loops run the same way, and what this leaves out is that the volume a chain needs is reached crop by crop; summed, the link overstates how soon several small crops together make a plant worthwhile.

connections.description: A plant draws its harvest from every grower within reach, on the island or off it, so growers elsewhere add to the volume that draws capacity near the island: GreenFood50 has its quinoa grown in the Netherlands and Belgium, close to its processing facilities, to cut transport (GreenFood50, n.d.), by its growers, most of the Dutch ones, working about 200 hectares for 600 tonnes a year (DutchNews.nl, 2026). More harvest within reach makes a plant or chain nearby more worthwhile, so buyers and processors build or keep capacity on or near the island rather than handle the crops elsewhere. In France, the firms that store, process and sell crops specialised in a few dominant ones for economies of scale, and their logistics are not adapted to sorting pulses out of mixed crops (Magrini et al., 2018, pp. 3, 9), and a small volume spread out or far from its users costs more to collect and to source (Meynard et al., 2018, pp. 7–8): the economies of scale hold wherever a chain is built, so the mechanism transfers. In the Netherlands, on Terschelling's saline field, producers of processed products are more concerned about volumes than the restaurants are, and stakeholders describe a chicken and egg: a producer needs a market, and a reliable market needs ample supply (ten Dam et al., 2023, pp. 10, 14); for quinoa, one expert says efforts only work with concentrated investments and high volumes (de Wit et al., 2022, p. 270). Years: a Zeeland quinoa chain was a project from 2021 to 2024 (De Vriend, 2024a): the delay sits in building the chain, not in the harvest, which follows within the year.
